title: What Portfolio Should You Look For in a Westchester Architect
excerpt: Choosing an architect in Westchester means reviewing more than pretty pictures. Here's what actually matters when you're evaluating someone to design your home project.
content:
When you're ready to hire an architect for your home project, you'll probably look at their portfolio first. That makes sense. But a lot of homeowners don't know what they're actually looking at, or what questions to ask about the work shown. A nice rendering or before-and-after photo doesn't tell you everything you need to know.

The portfolio matters, but it's just one piece of the puzzle. What you really want to understand is whether the architect understands your town, your home, and how to actually get the project built.

Look for Projects Similar to Yours

This sounds obvious, but it's easy to skip. If you're planning a kitchen remodel, look for examples of kitchen work. If you want a second-story addition, find projects where they've actually added a second story. A residential architect in Scarsdale working on historic homes should have examples of historic work. Someone handling new construction should show custom homes that actually got built, not just design concepts.

The reason this matters is simple. Every project type has its own demands. Adding a second story to an existing home requires different thinking than a new build. A bathroom renovation in Rye might face different site conditions than one in Larchmont. You want someone who has solved problems like yours before.

Pay Attention to the Process, Not Just the Pictures

When you review a portfolio, ask the architect to walk you through what happened. How did they approach the design? What challenges came up during construction? How did they solve them? The story behind a project tells you way more than the finished photos.

This is especially important in Westchester. Every municipality has its own building department and permit process. Your architect needs to know how things work in your specific town, whether that's White Plains, Tarrytown, or Eastchester. An architect who has pulled permits in multiple Westchester towns understands these differences and knows how to work with each one.

Make Sure Your Architect Can Actually Build What They Design

Here's something a lot of homeowners miss. Some architects design beautiful things that are incredibly hard or expensive to actually construct. You want someone who thinks about buildability from day one.

That's where the design-build approach in Westchester makes a real difference. When your architect is also a licensed general contractor, they're thinking about construction while they're drawing. No surprises during the build phase. No value engineering that compromises the design. Silvio Luca, the principal at House Architecture & Construction, holds both licenses. He runs every project personally, which means you're getting someone who understands design and construction equally well.

His portfolio includes home renovations in Westchester, additions, second-story work, kitchen and bathroom remodels, primary suite additions, historic restorations, open-concept conversions, and custom homes built from scratch. But more importantly, each of those projects went from concept to finished building. That's what actually matters.

Ask About Experience in Your Area

Mamaroneck and Bronxville have different character. Pelham and Harrison have different constraints. Scarsdale has different expectations. Your architect should understand your neighborhood and what fits.

When you're evaluating any portfolio, ask specifically about work done in your town. Not because the architect needs to work only in one place, but because it shows they understand local context and local processes.
